subjects.displayTitle: Sinai and the sacred call: images that awaken recognition
subjects.introduction: On the Mount of Knowledge Moses heard a voice that delighted his eyes, ignited his heart and expanded his breast, and Bahá’u’lláh says that the same voice is speaking now. The images of Exodus become, in his hands and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s, a vocabulary for recognition in the present: the fire in the blessed tree that was Moses’ own reality, Sinai astir with joy and sensing the fragrance of the garment, the land of allusions, the white hand as a heart renewed, the sacred valley crying out its presence. Joseph sold by his brothers and Jacob refreshed by the scent of a garment join the same language, lending words to separation and to sight restored. Exodus itself tells of a man who turned aside to look at a bush that burned without being consumed and was sent from that encounter to a suffering people [1]; the later symbolic uses are best read alongside that story rather than instead of it. The journey leads naturally to Moses himself, to the Torah and the Jewish people whose memory carries these images, and to the larger question of symbolism, of how a story becomes a language for an inward change that bears fruit.
subjects.arc: Begin with the call and the burning tree, follow Sinai into present recognition, and end with restored sight and the fruits of a response.

order.why: Enter the image of guidance within the burning tree.
shortened: His Holiness Moses beheld the luminous flame of divine guidance from the blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, and heard the divine call from that enkindled fire.

order.why: Open with a call that ignites the heart and enlarges the breast.
shortened: Hearken unto My call whereby We guided Moses on the Mount of Knowledge and caused him to hear that which delighted his eyes, ignited his heart, expanded his breast, and illumined his countenance.

order.why: Consider the tree interpreted through Moses’ own reality.
shortened: His Holiness Moses beheld the burning fire in the Blessed Tree, and thou hast beheld the burning fire in the Tree of Sanctification. Although that verdant Tree was the Reality of Moses wherein the fire of the love of God was ignited.

order.why: Interprets rods of earth, iron and gold as successive ways of training humanity.
Read the movement toward revelation and encounter.
Retain the reported comparison of God, speaker, and fire.
shortened: In the time of Moses, the ides of the Trinity was shown in (1) God, (2) the speaker of Mount Sinai, and (3) The Fire (which corresponds to our idea of the Holy Spirit).

order.why: Bring the ancient call into present recognition.
Read the repeated gift of hearing the call.
Hear Moses announce the Manifestation from the Mount of Knowledge.
shortened: O Ruhullah! Today the Spirit in the sacred valley cries "Here am I, O my God, here am I," and Moses on the Mount of Knowledge gives glad tidings of the Manifestation.

order.why: Consider Sinai itself portrayed as rejoicing.
Read the attraction of the call from Akka.
shortened: This is the day wherein the attraction of the Call that was raised from the direction of 'Akka hath seized Mount Sinai.

order.why: Turn from outward sight to inward contemplation.
Pause at the land of allusions.
Hear the summons to arise within the meeting of prophetic images.
shortened: O Salar-Ibrahim! The Friend and He Who conversed with God have come, and the Kingdom proclaimeth "The dominion belongeth unto God, the Possessor of existence!" The Mount hath attained to the presence of the Manifestation and hath cried out "Arise!

order.why: Consider sovereignty upon hearts and minds.
Read the linked names of Faran, Sinai, and Seir.
Retain the prayer for mountain and plain to be illumined.
Consider pilgrimage described through the sacred valley.
Answer the call through presence and praise.
shortened: Today in the wilderness of nearness unto the Spirit thou art crying "Here am I, here am I," and in the city of the love of Him Who conversed with God thou art uttering "Praise be unto Thee, O God of all the worlds."

order.why: Turn remembrance of protection into a prayer for others.
shortened: I beseech Thee by Thy Name through which Thou didst protect Him Who conversed with Thee from the evil of the Pharaoh of the age, to protect them that seek Thee from those who are moved by the winds of self and passion.

order.why: Ask for shielding and nearness through the remembered revelation.
Read the white hand as an image of a heart renewed.
Consider rescue from water as a language of consolation.
shortened: O namesake of Moses! The word "Moses" in Hebrew was "Moshi," meaning "drawn from the water," for Asiyih drew him from the water. Now you too should not be drowned in abundant weeping and floods of tears in the sea of grief, for the hand of the Asiyih of grace has lifted you up and saved you from drowning in heedlessness.

order.why: Read the Ark through tranquility and its angelic bearers.
Retain the psalm’s image of anointing.
shortened: ["It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments" Psalm 133:2]

order.why: Introduce the rejected Joseph.
shortened: Say: O people! Dust fill your mouths, and ashes blind your eyes, for having bartered away the Divine Joseph for the most paltry of prices.

order.why: Read the sale and the brothers’ weeping as renewed allusions.
shortened: And "they came to their father in the evening, weeping" hath been fulfilled, and "they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams" hath become manifest.

order.why: Turn toward Jacob refreshed by the fragrance of the garment.
shortened: How blessed thou art that in this divine Dispensation, in this century of God in which the power of His word hath moved the whole world thy conscience hath been revived and refreshed like unto Jacob's, in his eagerness with the scent of the garment of the true Joseph.

order.why: Revisit restored sight through the same image.
shortened: Give thanks to God that you have again become a sugar-breaking parrot, and like Jacob, your eyes were opened by the blessing of the garment, and you were perfumed by the fragrance of the divine Joseph's shirt.

order.why: Consider solitude transformed into companionship with God.
Join the fire of Sinai with the breezes of renewal.
Gather the prophetic images into a many-sided invitation to recognize.
Close the linked readings with recognition becoming active power.
Keep the fragment concerning the throne of revelation.
Retain the shared language of affliction and separation.
Return to the hope of unveiled vision.
End with steadfastness made visible through abundant fruits.
shortened: O thou who hast diffused the fragrances of truth! Stand thou firm in the Cause of God like unto a tree firmly rooted, with massive trunk, spreading branches and abundant fruits, that thou mayest become the manifestation of that which the glorious Lord hath said in the Gospel: "By their fruits ye shall know them."

order.why: Widen the invitation to hear across prophetic histories.

questions: What changes when Sinai and the burning tree become images of an encounter available to a present reader?
How does Exodus connect attention to a divine call with responsibility for people who are suffering?
What different aspects of spiritual experience are expressed by fire, fragrance, a white hand, and restored sight?
How can we honour the original narratives while exploring the later meanings given to their images?
What fruits in a person’s life might show that hearing has become a response?

neighbors.invitation: Compare fire, water, and spirit as images of love, knowledge, and bounty.
Explore sight restored as spiritual awakening.

references.label: 1 · Exodus 3:1–12 · The bush and the commission
references.note: Moses turns toward a bush that burns without being consumed, hears a call, and receives a commission connected to the suffering of the Israelites. Compare the relation between encounter and responsibility with the compilation’s later uses of Sinai and the flame.

subjects.displayTitle: Zoroaster and spiritual renewal: recognition across traditions
subjects.introduction: Zoroaster came from God with the fire of love ablaze in His hand, and the heedless failed to recognize Him. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answer to a questioner named Bahram opens a relationship rather than a history lesson: mix with the Zoroastrians, establish the foundation of love, rejoice that the Parsis have made their Prophet glad in heaven. Around that friendship gather accounts of Zoroaster’s appearance when Iran lay in ruins, of Gushtasp and Jamasp who spread His teaching, of the steed as a figure for spiritual journeying, and of a sapling growing again in the garden of Persian hopes after a thousand years of winter. Shared virtues, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá insists, are identical across the religions; only the social laws change with the age. The Gathas should be heard in their own voice: Yasna 30 calls its hearers to clear thought and a choice made in thought, word and action [1], an ethical summons that sits well beside this emphasis on virtue and freedom from self. The path continues into predictions and prophecies, progressive revelation, and the renewal of religion when its fire has grown dim.
subjects.arc: Begin with honour and friendship, explore the inheritance and its interpretations, and follow images of renewal toward ethical and spiritual response.

order.why: Open with Zoroaster’s divine mission and the fire of love.
shortened: O Bahram! Thou hast enquired about His Holiness Zoroaster. He came from God and summoned mankind to divine guidance. The fire of love was ablaze in His hand. Although he came with the fire of divine love and revealed the Book of laws and commandments, the heedless failed to apprehend His station and did not recognize His Revelation.

order.why: Place friendship with Zoroastrians at the outset.
Hear appreciation of the Parsi community’s devotion.
Consider the affection addressed to ancient Iranian friends.
shortened: O Parsee friends of 'Abdu'l-Baha! Every region has its ancient inhabitants as foundation and basis, and in every land there are original dwellers who are knowledgeable and aware. Those friends are the ancient Iranians and praise be to God, in these days they are companions and intimates of 'Abdu'l-Baha.

order.why: Read the response to a question about Zoroaster’s place in the writings.
Retain the interpretation of the Companions of the Rass.
Read the account of dating with its stated uncertainty about histories.
Preserve the account of travel and prophetic encounters.
shortened: The nest and dwelling place of all the Prophets, even His Holiness Zoroaster that great one also made a journey to these regions and met with some of the Prophets of Israel.

order.why: Keep the reported description of language and scripture in its historical voice.
Read the narrative of Zoroaster’s influence in Iran.
shortened: Among the holy Manifestations of God was Zoroaster. His prophethood is as clear and evident as the sun, His proof is effulgent, His evidence manifest, and His testimony decisive. When Zoroaster appeared, Iran was in ruins and the people of Iran were in utmost degradation.
In brief, Iran was encompassed by the darkness of humiliation and abasement. It was at such a time that Zoroaster appeared. He illumined Iran and awakened and enlightened the Iranian people.

order.why: Consider the role assigned to Gushtasp and Jamasp.
Explore the steed as a metaphor for spiritual movement.
Attend to the explanation of a passage and its wording.
Read the account of opposition with attention to its polemical setting.
shortened: Do not be saddened or grieved by the actions of some foolish ones, for expecting consciousness from the proud is like expecting sunlight from the dark night - this is impossible and unattainable. The actions of this group are like the savagery of wolves and the sting of scorpions. They are steeped in pride and are leaders of evil people - what can be expected of them? It was these former leaders who issued the death sentence for Zoroaster and laid waste to Iran. In every age and time when the light of truth dawned, the leaders arose in denial and sought to resist the light of truth.

order.why: Retain the criticism of priests and the appeal concerning Jamshid’s work.
shortened: It is hoped that all will become conscious, for the unfaithful priests have altered more or less the blessed book of Zand to remove the glad tidings of today. Know truly that the spirit of the great Zoroaster seeks refuge with the Lord from these sinful priests. See how faithless they are. And if the friends' hands are cut off from the work of the Master Jamshid, endless disorder will result. The Master should not accept this, for the friends strived in his work with heart and soul and with complete truthfulness and uprightness.

order.why: Notice the distinction drawn between obstructive and wise religious leaders.
shortened: We smiled, we wept - both from joy, for the Persian friends have become so enkindled that they have forgotten the thousand-year-old lethargy and wilting, and have become pure and free from the contamination of the thoughts of ignorant priests. The wise priests are the candles of the gathering and the sweet-singing birds of the rose garden and meadow. They are the guides on Hoshidar's path and the light of the world of life-giving Bahram. In any case, the hope from the Sun of the celestial realm is that all the Persians of that country become the lords of the universe and the stars of the eternal heaven.

order.why: Turn toward seeing and hearing as spiritual responses.
Discusses Zoroastrian and Israelite attachment to names in contrast with recognizing one spiritual reality.
Introduce the seed, rain, and harvest of a revelation.
shortened: The pure seed that His Holiness Zoroaster scattered sprouted with the rain of heavenly bounty and the field became green and verdant. The time of harvest arrived and it became a celestial blessing.

order.why: Consider a spark becoming a mountain of fire.
Read the named figures of promised renewal.
shortened: The radiant Mehr Hushidar of the divine world was the sun of the bright sphere that gave adornment to the garden of existence. And after him Bahram will illuminate his countenance and reveal his face, and will bring the world of spirit and heart under his signet ring, and will place the crown of divine kingship of the world, and will put on his head the blessed diadem of heavenly glory.

order.why: Consider recognition interpreted as response to Zoroaster’s counsel.
Read fulfillment as fidelity to a covenant. Revisit the interpretation of covenant and fulfillment.
Keep the reported claim concerning prophecy distinct from direct scriptural evidence.
shortened: The prophecies of the Zoroastrian (Norserry) plainly foretell the coming of the Bab and the Blessed Perfection, so in large number they have become believers, thought don't believe nor do they accept either the Bible or the Koran.

order.why: Consider decline and renewed hope within the address to a correspondent.
Read the imagery of a guiding star.
Hear the invitation to joy and celebration.
shortened: O Zoroastrian friends! Every people among the peoples had their day of triumph, and on that day they held great festivities and established feasts of joy and delight. Today is your day, it is your time of joy and gladness, for the Persian Sun hath shone forth from the horizon of Iran and cast its rays upon all regions. Ere long Iran shall become the envy of the world and the Iranians shall become the object of the world's admiration.

order.why: Consider remembrance as a new day of thanksgiving.
Read joy that becomes a source of happiness for others.
Retain the reported proclamation to Persian Zoroastrians.
shortened: To the Persian Zoroastrian say: Awake, Awake! For the sun of your salvation hath arisen from the horizon of Persia. Ere long the ancient glory of your native land shall return, you will be honored amongst all the nations of the earth. Shake off your sleep! Ahuramazda has come and he shall make this world a paradise and its inhabitants the angels of heaven.'

order.why: Follow the promised renewal toward a vision of humanity’s unity.
shortened: For many centuries the sun of Persia had set; but it has now arisen with iridescent rays from the East of the Placeless. The luminary of their ancient glory and majesty has again dawned. Sousheyanss has come and instead of unifying only Persia, he is the Unifier of mankind. The Parsee community must greatly rejoice, for their Promised One hath come.

order.why: Close the linked readings with an inward victory over self and passion.
Retain the further account of travel and the Caucasus.
Consider the reported preservation of books in India.
Keep the account of endurance and recognition with its attribution.
shortened: The teachings of Moses were like a seed, but when the seed grew into a plant and bore blossom, then fruit--the fruit signified Christ, who was the result of all the teachings of Moses... As to the Manifestation (Baha'u'llah) all the religious books in the world bear witness to Him. The Magis have resisted the Mohammedans for nearly 1,400 years, refusing to accept Mohammedanism, and suffered great persecutions. They accept and believe in the manifestation (Baha'u'llah) because of the prophecies of their books.

order.why: Read the supplied prophecy concerning three periods of stillness.
shortened: Thou hadst written concerning the "stopping of the sun", that in the book of the Zoroastrians it is recorded that at the end of the cycle it is ordained that this "stopping" shall occur in three Manifestations: in the first, the sun will remain ten days at the meridian of the heaven; in the second, twenty days; and in the third, thirty days.

And as to thy third question -- whether the appearance of His Holiness Zoroaster was before Moses or after -- Zoroaster was of those Prophets who were raised up after Moses; and this, moreover, is established by the explicit texts of history.

order.why: Return to the image of a sapling and spiritual spring.
shortened: In brief, the purpose is that praise be to God, in the garden of the Persians' hopes an incomparable sapling is growing with utmost power and might from the sprinklings of the cloud of bounty, the heat of the Sun of Truth, and the blowing of the breezes of eternal glory. Eternal grace and heavenly bounty have caused this sapling to grow again in Iran.

A new cycle has come, fresh life has been attained. That spiritual spring which for a thousand years until now had passed through seasons of summer, autumn and winter, has come again with utmost freshness and grace with the hosts of divine bounty...

order.why: End with the extended distinction between shared virtues and changing social laws.
shortened: Answer: The religions of God have the same foundation, but the dogmas appearing later have differed. Each of the divine religions has two aspects. The first is essential. It concerns morality and development of the virtues of the human world. This aspect is common to all. It is fundamental; it is one; there is no difference, no variation in it. As regards the inculcation of morality and the development of human virtues, there is no difference whatsoever between the teachings of Zoroaster, Jesus and Baha'u'llah. In this they agree; they are one. The second aspect of the divine religions is nonessential. It concerns human needs and undergoes change in every cycle according to the exigency of the time.

Therefore, the nonessentials which deal with details of community are changed according to the exigency of the time and conditions. But the essential foundation of the teachings of Moses, Zoroaster, Jesus and Baha'u'llah is identical, is one; there is no difference whatsoever.

questions: What might it mean to approach another tradition through friendship as well as through ideas about its history or prophecies?
How does Yasna 30’s attention to thought and choice enrich the discussion of spiritual recognition?
What is gained by distinguishing a tradition’s own scriptures from later accounts and interpretations of it?
How do fire, seed, harvest, and springtime illuminate different aspects of renewal?
How might an affirmation of shared virtues coexist with careful attention to differences in belief and practice?

neighbors.invitation: Consider wishing for another’s welfare for their own sake.
Compare fire in a sacred tree as language for an inward reality.

references.label: 1 · Yasna 30:2–3 · Hearing, thought, and choice
references.note: The Gathic passage calls for attentive hearing and clear thought, then presents a choice between better and bad in thought, word, and action. Compare this ethical summons with the compilation’s reflections on virtues. Its own religious setting should remain distinct from later Bahá’í interpretations of Zoroastrian prophecy.

subjects.displayTitle: Remembering early Islam: fellowship, trial, and division
subjects.introduction: Two Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, had killed one another for generations; within a few years of hearing Muhammad they were brothers, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to that reversal as the plainest sign of what a Manifestation of God does to human hearts. The early history of Islam holds that transformation and its undoing: torment in Mecca, flight to Medina, the trench dug against besieging enemies, lukewarm believers who doubted even as the Prophet struck the boulder, and then, after His passing, quarrels over authority that turned a few words into swords and ended in the blood of Karbila. The Qur’an asks its hearers to remember the grace by which hostile hearts were joined [1], and that remembrance is the measure against which every later division must be weighed. Harsh judgments on particular adversaries belong to their own moment, not to whole peoples now. What the history leaves open is how faith overcomes hatred rather than feeding it, a question that leads on to the life of Muhammad, the martyrdom of Imam Husayn, and the lessons the past still has to teach.
subjects.arc: Begin with enemies becoming brothers, follow persecution and migration, face accounts of violence and division, and return to practical trust and the overcoming of hatred.

order.why: Open with the transformation of hostile tribes into brothers.
Read the remembered spread of guidance through the Hijaz.
shortened: At one time, the holy divine fragrances perfumed that land and region, and the call of the Beauty of Muhammad was raised from all sides and directions of the Hijaz, and that Orb of Guidance had risen from that Batha horizon, and heavenly sustenance was being sent down.

order.why: Retain the historical rhetoric of social transformation in its source voice.
Consider the reported youthful encounter with a monk.
shortened: When Mohamad travelled with his uncle Abou Talib, as far as Bostra and met the Christian Monk Sergius, or as the Mohamadan name him Boheira, he was only eleven years old and stayed one night in the monastery.

order.why: Follow persecution into migration.
Recounts early persecution and migration while explaining the defensive character of Muhammad’s military expeditions.
Distinguish the migrations to Medina and Abyssinia in the reported account.
Read reassurance amid danger and its later interpretation.
Enter the account of defensive preparations.
shortened: At one time during His migration journey, while surrounded by enemies who were exerting their utmost in reducing the believers and in this regard were succeeding, the Prophet Muhammad ordered a moat to be dug so they could hide therein.

order.why: Consider doubt and confidence during collective danger.
shortened: When His Holiness was striking the boulder with His staff, some of the munafiqin were remarking to their lukewarm friends [among the believers], "Out of our fear, not a sign of our courage, we wet ourselves. Therefore, how can He speak so boldly?" Which is why the following verse has been revealed, "God shall mock them, and keep them long in their rebellion, wandering in perplexity."

In this battle the number of defenders were seven hundred, of which nearly three hundred were either of the munafiqin or lukewarm in their convictions. But when they reached the Ayvan-i Kasraw and saw the divine prophecies fulfilled, they were all ashamed and remorseful.

order.why: Read the further account of fragile loyalty under pressure.
shortened: In the days of the Prophet--may my spirit be a sacrifice unto Him--despite the spread of power in Yathrib, in a single day a great multitude from the Bani Zafar tribe, with their families and children, apostatized and joined the enemy. In the Battle of the Confederates, on the Day of the Trench, when affliction and severe hunger intensified, the companions of the Prophet--who numbered close to six or seven hundred--three hundred showed hypocrisy.

order.why: Retain the reported explanation of warfare in its historical context.
Read the narratives of Hunayn and Banu Qurayza without merging their episodes.
Place the further account of the massacre beside the other narratives.
Hear the distress caused by reading the account of Banu Qurayza.
shortened: In my childhood, this wronged one read in a book by Mulla Baqir Majlisi about the raid on the Banu Qurayzah. From that moment I was distressed and full of sorrow, to the extent that my pen cannot express it -- even though what happened was the decree of God, and its intent was only to foil oppressors.

order.why: Attend to the declared purpose of removing hatred and contention.
Introduce the account of Ghadir-i-Khum.
Read the recollection of division around the Prophet’s final illness.
Keep the interpretation of the disputed statement nearby.
shortened: This statement was the first breach in Islam and was the saying of the second Caliph who said "The Book of God is sufficient for us," as mentioned in Bukhari which is considered an authentic book of hadith by the Sunnis.

order.why: Follow the extended lament over authority, conflict, and loss. Read the further lament over words that become instruments of division.
shortened: The words "Sufficient unto us is the Book of God" became as a piercing blade that cleft the head of the Prince of the faithful; it became the trenchant sword that was wielded by the son of the "Eater of Livers."   These words kindled a raging fire on the "Night of Clangour"  and caused four thousand memorizers of the Qur'an, the most prominent companions of 'Ali, to turn into the wretched rabble of the Seceders.   These words scattered the ranks of the believers and divided the lines of the faithful.  These words changed the affection of the lovers of the Muhammadan Beauty into swords and spears, into injury and enmity.  These words became a dagger of hatred and, in the land of Taff,  lacerated the throat of that luminous beauty,  staining the earth with his blessed blood.  These words brought about that most great disaster and most profound disgrace on the plain of Karbila.

order.why: Distinguish outward devotion from intention at Karbila.
shortened: Even the hateful company of the oppressors in the desert of Karbila, showed an outward semblance of devotion to Him, but although they made mention of Him with words yet in reality they were insincere, ill-intentioned, and deceitful.

order.why: Read the contrast between professed courage and actual conduct.
Consider the different meanings attributed to victory.
shortened: His Holiness the Messenger in the Battle of Badr struck off the heads of the opposers and was victorious. The Prince of Martyrs in Karbala had his body torn to pieces, yet was still victorious, for "verily it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers."

order.why: Read the reported destruction and restoration of places of remembrance.
shortened: They razed to dust the site of martyrdom in Karbila and Najaf, then plowed it under. For nearly eighty years they plowed and planted crops so that no trace would remain. After eighty years, people came and said: "Yes, it was here." They built up that site of martyrdom. This was in the time of the Umayyads. Then when the Abbasids came, they built it up. In the time of Mutawakkil they destroyed it again and cultivated crops for nearly two hundred years.

order.why: Compare the pursuit of fame with enduring spiritual memory.
shortened: Thirty-six persons sat upon the throne of the caliphate, and all were bound to name and fame, yet of none of them does any trace or sign remain. But because Bahlul was known as the madman of God, they are still building domes and shrines in his honor.

order.why: Retain the account of worldly success with its attribution.
shortened: Today I read in history about Ibn Mashtub in Diyar Bakr, who was among the most fortunate of early Muslim kings, blessed with every means of success. Throughout his reign, no event occurred that caused him distress. His domains were in utmost security and peace. He waged several battles against the Crusaders and was victorious in all encounters.

order.why: Include the brief anecdotal introduction without supplying missing events.
shortened: In the days of the Prophet, there was one named Nu'man who was quite mischievous, and one named Mu'ayth who was dark of countenance. The Prince of the Faithful was engaged in battle with one of the tribes and appointed Mu'ayth as storekeeper.

order.why: Close the linked readings with care, preparation, and reliance upon God.
Return to the supplied account of siege and hunger.
shortened: In the battle of Khandag the enemies hordes rushed forward and besieged the city Medina. Mohamad and his companions were in the town and had no other recou[rse] but to defend it. The prophet's uncle being amongst the enemies cut all the [ways] of communication and the innocent inhabitants were on the verge of starv[ation.] All the foodstuffs were consumed and the animals killed to appease the appetite of the people.

order.why: Preserve the brief reference to accounts of Hajjaj.
Consider the anecdote that contrasts appearance with character.
Retain the supplied polemical interpretation with its explicit provisional translation authority.
shortened: Convey my greetings and praise to that distinguished person, and mention that in regard to the Qa'im, the truth lay with the Sunnis, for the Desired One appeared from physical descent in accordance with their beliefs, while the Shi'ih divines have been and continue to be in error from the beginning of Islam until now. Even now they await the appearance of an imaginary person from an imaginary Jabulqa.

The likes of these turbaned ones that are seen today, together with Ja'far and his sons before them, have led the helpless people astray and cast them into the well of vain imaginings. The Sun is shining and manifest, yet they shut their eyes and blindly search for Jabulqa and Jabulsa.

order.why: End with an act of protection becoming a path to faith.

questions: What conditions allow former enemies to become a community, and what can cause that fellowship to unravel?
How does the Qur’anic appeal to unity illuminate the accounts of division gathered here?
What responsibilities do readers have when comparing reported conversations, theological interpretations, and accounts of violent events?
How can we examine particular conflicts without extending blame to whole religious or ethnic communities?
What do the stories of protection, practical care, and professed loyalty suggest about faith becoming visible in conduct?

neighbors.invitation: Apply the concern for another’s welfare to the responsibilities of rulers.
Consider the careful distinctions between recognition, good deeds, and wrongdoing.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 3:103 · From enmity to fellowship
references.note: The verse calls its hearers to hold together, avoid division, and remember the grace through which hostile hearts became joined. Compare that summons with the collection’s accounts of fellowship and later conflict. It supplies an ethical point of comparison, not independent confirmation of every historical detail.

subjects.displayTitle: Spiritual baptism: a new life bearing new fruit
subjects.introduction: To be born of water and the Spirit, as Jesus told Nicodemus one night, is not to re-enter the womb but to receive a life the body cannot give [1]. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads that saying as a key: the spirit is divine grace, the water is knowledge and life, and the fire is the love of God, and material water, however it cleanses the body, cannot touch the heart. Real baptism is the soul’s purification from anger, pride, deceit and self-love, received when the teachings themselves pour over a person like living water. The fire burns away the veil between us and heavenly realities, and those set alight by it become a new people who, He hopes, will make the world new in turn, discarding old garments, old politics founded on war, old ideas. The question that follows is practical: whether insight has produced generosity, and whether a renewed heart can unite others. From here the way opens toward the second birth, the Holy Spirit, and the transformation of the soul by the divine elixir.
subjects.arc: Begin with renewal that changes the world, explore water, spirit, and fire, and test the meaning of new birth through character and service.

order.why: Introduce the Gospel language of water, Spirit, and fire. Retain the explanation that joins water and fire through life-giving love.
shortened: Water is the cause of life, and when Christ speaks of water, He is symbolizing that which is the cause of Everlasting Life.
This life-giving water of which He speaks is like unto fire, for it is none other than the Love of God, and this love means life to our souls.

By the fire of the Love of God the veil is burnt which separates us from the Heavenly Realities, and with clear vision we are enabled to struggle onward and upward, ever progressing in the paths of virtue and holiness, and becoming the means of light to the world.

order.why: Open with the expansive vision of a new people and a more peaceful world. Return to the vision of changed faces and characters.
Read the purposes assigned to Christ’s appearance.
shortened: Nay, rather, Christ appeared in order to illumine the world of humanity, to render the earthly world celestial, to make the human kingdom a realm of angels, to unite the hearts, to enkindle the light of love in human souls, so that such souls might become independent, attaining complete unity and fellowship, turning to God, entering into the divine Kingdom, receiving the bounties and bestowals of God and partaking of the manna from heaven. Through Christ they were intended to be baptized by the Holy Spirit, attain a new spirit and realize the everlasting life.

order.why: Explains baptism through water of life, the Holy Spirit and the fire of divine love.
Study repentance as the essence of baptism. Study the extended interpretation of spirit, water, and fire. Consider the stated Bahá’í position on the outward symbol.
shortened: Answer: The essence of baptism is purification by repentance.

Therefore, by spirit is meant divine grace; by water, knowledge and life; and by fire, the love of God. For material water cleanses not the heart of man but his body. Rather, the heavenly water and spirit, which are knowledge and life, cleanse and purify the heart of man.
But in the Dispensation of Baha'u'llah this symbol is no longer required, for its reality, which is to be baptized with the spirit and the love of God, has been established and realized.

order.why: Distinguish bodily cleansing from the soul’s response to teachings.
Read the three images through knowledge, love, and bounty.
Turn that interpretation into prayer for confirmation.
Consider gratitude for illumination and life.
Connect baptism with a second birth.
shortened: Praise be to God that thou hast experienced the second birth from the darkness of the world of nature and hast been baptized with the fire of love, the water of life, and the breathings of the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Explore the analogy of birth from the womb of nature.
Read new birth through the acquisition of divine qualities.
shortened: The new birth is realized in this Kingdom when we become characterized by the characteristics of God, when His Name and attributes become our names and attributes.
The New Birth is when the imperfections by which we are surrounded are wholly overcome and we are completely purified from all the evil of the world.

order.why: Locate its significance in virtues and spiritual life.
shortened: The spirit and intelligence of man is essential, and that is the manifestation of divine virtues, the merciful bestowals of God, the eternal life and baptism through the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Retain the reported account of three baptisms with its source status.
shortened: There are three baptisms spoken of by the prophets: the baptism of water, of spirit and of fire. The first signifies the condition when the soul receives the teachings of the knowledge of God. The second, when the soul receives the spirit; when the soul receives this baptism the spirit speaks through him, he has no need to be taught of men or to ask questions, because the holy spirit will enlighten and teach him. The third baptism is that of fire, when the soul becomes aflame with the love of God and insensible to any other attraction.

order.why: Keep the brief parallel explanation alongside it. Place the further reported formulation beside it.
Read the reported criticism of ritual practice as an interpretation.
Retain the shorter reported criticism.
shortened: The Baptism of the Christians as practiced today is not the teachings of Christ. Baptism by John the Baptist was only a symbol used to signify that the hearts had been purified by repentance (they were grown people, not children).

order.why: Preserve the brief statement without inventing its missing context.
shortened: This great power is that of the Holy Spirit. It is the divine power which transforms a stone into a diamond, which changes darkness into light, which saves man from the world of defects and enables him to attain the world of virtues. This is possible only through baptism by the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Read the prayer for sight, hearing, and spiritual baptism.
Consider joy and life renewed through the divine call.
Retain the account of those present receiving spirit and love.
shortened: Those in attendance were baptized with the divine spirit and the fire of the love of God.

order.why: Follow renewal into the sea and spirit of love.
Close the linked readings with gratitude joined to continued effort.
Read birth and resurrection through recognition in each dispensation.
shortened: Even as Jesus said: "Ye must be born again." Again He saith: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." The purport of these words is that whosoever in every dispensation is born of the Spirit and is quickened by the breath of the Manifestation of Holiness, he verily is of those that have attained unto "life" and "resurrection" and have entered into the "paradise" of the love of God.

order.why: Read preparation of the stream bed as purification of the heart.
Retain the pilgrim account of stages of birth.
Keep the disputed attribution together with the supplied correction rejecting it.
Read the provisional translation concerning the human spirit.
shortened: The human spirit is the rational soul, that is, the one that perceives the realities of things, discovers them and encompasses them. It has brilliant effects, radiant lights, penetrating power and perfect ability, distinguished in all its conditions and concept from other spirits. It is baptized by water and spirit.

order.why: Distinguish general uses of spirit from the life of faith.
shortened: This human spirit, which is the rational soul, encompasses all things, discovers all things, and comprehends all things.

But when spiritual people speak of the spirit, they do not mean this spirit. They mean that eternal spirit, that life of faith, that spirit of which Christ says man must be baptized with it, and until he is baptized with that spirit he cannot enter the Kingdom of God.

order.why: Consider the spirit of faith as an impulse toward virtues.
shortened: There is still another power which is differentiated from that of the soul and mind. This third power is the spirit which is an emanation from the divine bestower; it is the effulgence of the sun of reality, the radiation of the celestial world, the spirit of faith, the spirit His Holiness the Christ refers to when he says, "Those that are born of the flesh are flesh, and those that are born of the spirit are spirit."
This spirit of faith is the flame of reality, the life of humanity and the cause of eternal illumination. It inspires man to attain the virtues and perfections of the divine world.

order.why: Read its quickening power through the rays of the sun.
shortened: There is, however, another Spirit, which may be termed the Divine, to which Jesus Christ refers when He declares that man must be born of its quickening and baptized with its living fire. Souls deprived of that Spirit are accounted as dead, though they are possessed of the human spirit.
This quickening spirit emanates spontaneously from the Sun of Truth, from the reality of Divinity, and is not a revelation or a manifestation. It is like the rays of the sun.

order.why: Read the prayer for freedom from worldly stains.
shortened: I beg of God that thou mayest be baptized by the baptism of Baha'u'llah and become free from all the stains of the mortal world and that thou mayest take delight in the favors of God in the paradise of unity, and that thou mayest be able to become pleasing to God and mayest appear with thy face illuminated as a candle in the world of eternity.

order.why: Consider renewal as a received bounty.
shortened: But ye, praise be to God, are at present especially favored with this bounty, have become of the chosen, have been informed of the heavenly instructions, have gained admittance into the Kingdom of God, have become the recipients of unbounded blessings and have been baptized with the Water of Life, with the fire of the love of God and with the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Read the call of the Kingdom as regeneration.
shortened: The call of the Abha Kingdom penetrates swiftly like spirit through veins, arteries, hearts and souls, creating a new creation and baptizing with water, spirit and fire. A second birth takes place and a new creation is raised up.

order.why: Consider life freed from oppression and heedlessness.
shortened: Today the pulsating power in the arteries of the body of the world is the spirit of the Covenant—the spirit which is the cause of life. Whosoever is vivified with this spirit the freshness and beauty of life become manifest in him, he is baptized with the Holy Spirit, he is born again, is freed from oppression and tyranny, from heedlessness and harshness which deaden the spirit, and attains to everlasting life.

order.why: Move toward the bond of unity among peoples.
shortened: It is the spirit that makes man heavenly; it is the spirit that makes man recipient of the Holy Spirit's breaths; it is the spirit that discovers the realities of things; it is the spirit that has produced all these effects; it is the spirit that has established all sciences; it is the spirit that bestows eternal life; it is the spirit that unites different nations; it is the spirit that brings together East and West; it is the spirit that makes the human world divine. Therefore, those souls who are recipients of the power of the spirit are the cause of life to the world.

order.why: End with renewed people cultivating the field of humanity.
shortened: I hope that you may become baptized with the Fire of the Love of God and the Water of the Holy Spirit, and that each of you may become a Divine Farmer and sow in the farm of humanity the seeds of reality, irrigating them with the Waters of the Teacings of Baha'u'llah, so that the Light of Truth may illumine that country.

order.why: Return to the supplied Gospel saying and its accompanying citations.

questions: What relationships emerge among knowledge, love, grace, and the purification of character?
How does John’s conversation with Nicodemus challenge a merely physical understanding of new birth?
What differences remain between a scriptural narrative, a Bahá’í interpretation of it, and the practices of other communities?
How should the collection’s explicit correction of an attribution affect the way we use reported explanations?
What fruits of spiritual renewal might be visible in a person’s capacity to serve, reconcile, or bring people together?

neighbors.invitation: Consider helping another heart to be illumined as a mark of a fruitful life.
Compare spiritual sight and eternal life with the significance attributed to outward wonders.

references.label: 1 · John 3:1–8 · Nicodemus and the new birth
references.note: Nicodemus asks how a person can be born again; Jesus distinguishes birth of flesh from birth of Spirit and speaks of water and Spirit. Compare the dialogue with the interpretations collected here, without assuming that every Christian understanding of baptism is identical to the Bahá’í account.

subjects.displayTitle: Miracles: wonder, evidence, and the opening of insight
subjects.introduction: Asked about the wonders attributed to Bahá’u’lláh, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá declined to recount them, not because they were untrue but because a report proves nothing to someone who was not there, and every tradition has such reports. If these are hearsay so are those, and even an eyewitness may wonder whether he saw a miracle or a trick. That argument is sharpened by a story: a stranger asks ‘Alí to prove his trust in God by leaping from a roof, and is told that the servant does not test the Master. Faith that is compelled by a spectacle is not faith, which must come through insight and recognition. Most miracles, besides, carry an inner meaning, as when the blind are given sight,. John’s account of the man born blind, with its refusal to assign blame, sits alongside these interpretations of healing [1]. The journey leads on to the proofs of the Manifestations of God, to the resurrection of Christ, and to the question of literal and symbolic interpretation that underlies them all.
subjects.arc: Begin with the problem of evidence, distinguish possibility from proof, explore inner meanings, and end with the practical significance of teachings and transformation.

order.why: Open with the extended inquiry into testimony, proof, and inner meaning.
shortened: But these accounts cannot be a decisive proof and testimony for all, since the hearer might say that they are not factually true, as the followers of other denominations also recount miracles from their leaders.  For instance, Hindus recount certain miracles of Brahma.  How can we know that those are false and that these are true?  If these are reported accounts, so too are those; if these are widely attested, then the same holds true of those.  Thus such accounts do not constitute a sufficient proof.  Of course, a miracle may be a proof for the eyewitness, but even then he might not be sure whether what he beheld was a true miracle or mere sorcery.
Moreover, most of the miracles attributed to the Prophets have an inner meaning.

order.why: Focus on the difference between presence and absence.
shortened: But in the Sacred Scriptures a special terminology is used, and in the sight of the Manifestations of God these marvels and miracles are of no importance, so much so that They do not even wish them to be mentioned. For even if these miracles were considered the greatest of proofs, they would constitute a clear evidence only for those who were present when they took place, not for those who were absent.

order.why: Compare the reception of miracle claims across communities.
shortened: This kind of proof is always for the believer. A Buddhist will not be convinced by these proofs, they are convincing as far as the orthodox Jews are concerned because they believe in Moses. On the other hand the miracles which are attributed to Jesus Christ are only proofs for the Christians. The Jews refute them as a whole. No one lives today who has seen these miracles performed by Christ, so that they may bear testimony to them. Likewise they attribute many miracles to Mohamed - those miracles are only accepted by the Mohammedans and not by the Jews and the Christians.

order.why: Explains why reported miracles convince followers of one religion but are disputed by others.
Consider the reader in a future century.
Read the demand for consistency in judging different traditions.
Distinguish limited comprehension from proof of impossibility.
Retain the reported affirmation of divine possibility.
Ask what function a Messenger comes to fulfil.
Examine demands that make belief depend upon a chosen spectacle.
shortened: And if proof is intended, proof must be universal, not particular, else matters would degenerate into children's games and the gathering of mysteries would become a magician's arena. For if every soul had a whim, then the Guide of nations would have to become, among all peoples, the plaything of every mindless and uncomprehending one. And surely you would not consent to this.

order.why: Read the story of testing and the further reply to such demands.
shortened: It is related that one day His Holiness the Prince of Believers (Ali), peace be upon him, was on the edge of a roof when a stranger submitted: "O Ali, are you confident in God's protection, preservation and safeguarding?" He replied: "How could I not be, when I am the first believer in God?" The man submitted: "Then rely on God's protection and throw yourself from the edge of the roof." He responded: "The higher must test the lower, not anyone testing anyone else anywhere. The Master has the right to test the servant, but the servant has no right to test the Master."

This is why when seven tribes from among the Arab tribes came before His Holiness the Messenger (may my spirit be sacrificed for him), and each demanded a miracle as a test - one saying "until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us," another uttering "or you bring down a book from heaven," another saying "or you have a house of gold," another uttering "or you ascend into heaven" - since their purpose was to test, the answer to all was "Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"

order.why: Keep the parallel account with its remaining source omission.
shortened: In the Quran it is mentioned that seven tribes came before the Secret of Being and Essence of Purpose, His Holiness Muhammad, peace be upon Him. Each made his faith contingent upon a miracle. One said: "Bring down a book from heaven." Another said: "Cast down a fragment of heaven to earth." Another said: "Make a spring to flow." Another said: "Ascend to heaven." Another said: "Show us the Lord with His hosts." Another said: "Produce a treasure." Another said: "Bring forth the lofty paradise." In reply to all of these He declares: "Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I aught but a mortal messenger?"...

order.why: Consider the distinction between insight and compelled belief.
shortened: "In God's sight, forced belief is not acceptable. Consider - is a forced friendship acceptable to you? If you tell someone 'If you don't believe, I will kill you' and they believe, this is not faith. Faith must be through recognition, through insight, through guidance, through the diffusion of divine fragrances, through the dawning of lights.

order.why: Introduce healing as spiritual awakening.
shortened: They say our Lord cured blindness; it was blindness of the soul. ("They have eyes and see not, ears they have and hear not.") He brought on spiritual awakening.

order.why: Read the relation between possibility and the metaphor of sight.
Retain the reported interpretation of dust and spittle.
Keep the concise spiritual interpretation with its attribution.
Read the contrast between a physical cure and a greater spiritual effect.
shortened: If healing the lame and crippled is a miracle, it can also be produced by a dose of medicine. This is no great achievement.

order.why: Consider the story about the limits of influence upon obstinacy.
shortened: It is recorded in one of the Books of the Mussulman that one day Jesus Christ was seen fleeing to the mountains, and some one asked Him why He was fleeing away. He said, "I am running away from a foolish man." He was asked, "Are you not Christ? Why do you not bestow upon him the great Spirit?" Jesus answered, "God has given Me a Spirit, the power of which will open the eyes of the blind and cause the deaf to hear, but it has no effect upon the mind of a foolish person."

order.why: Place the parallel reported story beside it.
shortened: Christ said:- "With the same breath of the Holy Spirit that I blew over the ignorant and he became wise; the deaf became hearing, the blind seeing, the mute speaking, the sick became well and the dead received a new life - I blew the same breath of the holy Spirit more than one thousand times over this fool and there was no result; consequently I am flying away from him.

order.why: Turn toward constancy as evidence.
shortened: Another proof and evidence of the truth of this Revelation, which amongst all other proofs shineth as the sun, is the constancy of the eternal Beauty in proclaiming the Faith of God.

order.why: Read steadfast presence under opposition.
Consider a Cause advancing despite imprisonment.
shortened: What miracle could be greater than this - that He raised up His Cause while in the Most Great Prison under chains and moved both East and West. This is just one miracle of Baha'u'llah's miracles.

order.why: Hear the personal account of an apparently impossible journey.
Close the linked readings with knowledge and human well-being.
Retain the explicit distinction between interpretation and denial of possibility.
Read the challenge to a single explanation of suffering.
Read the Báb’s supplied account with its particular wording.
Consider the reported account of the creative word.
shortened: Jesus said: "Arise, take up thy bed and walk." He did not use prayers or mental suggestion. He used spiritual authority in the command which was the power of the Holy Spirit manifest in him. Therefore his word was obeyed because it was creative.

order.why: Revisit the challenge of evidence across time.
shortened: As the miracles and the extraordinary signs of the Manifestation will not be proof for the centuries to come after this, we have not mentioned them. The miracles are only proof for those who are present, not for those who are to come, for the idolaters have also recorded miracles, on the part of their gods, in their books.

order.why: Consider how wonders may become a veil to teachings.
shortened: The miracles which appeared through the Manifestation the Master did not like to mention, because they will not be proof to others. They were only a demonstration for those who witnessed them.

While the miracles which actually appeared in the time of the Manifestation are greater than all, the Master did not wish to mention them, for the Manifestation said that the miracles would be like a veil over the people, for, in every time, the proofs (of this Word) will be so evident and clear the people can understand them.

order.why: Hear the warning about what can obscure the message.
End by asking what it means actually to practise a teaching.
Read the wider invitation to wonder at phenomena.
Consider the stated relation between causal law and divine power.
Consider possibility and mystery through the discussion of Christ’s birth.
shortened: The operation of miracles is not necessarily irrational or illogical. It does by no means constitute a limitation of the Omnipotence of God. The belief in the possibilities of miracles, on the contrary, implies that God's power is beyond any limitation whatsoever. For it is only logical to believe that the Creator, Who is the sole Author of all the laws operating in the universe, is above them and can, therefore, if He deems it necessary, alter them at His Own Will. We, as humans, cannot possibly attempt to read His Mind, and to fully grasp His Wisdom. Mystery is therefore an inseparable part of true religion, and as such, should be recognized by the believers.

order.why: Retain the further clarification of the Bahá’í position.
Read the parallel pilgrim account with its source status.

questions: What is the difference between regarding an event as possible, believing a report of it, and treating it as decisive evidence?
How can we assess miracle claims consistently across traditions, including our own?
What does John’s account of the man born blind add to the discussion of healing, responsibility, and spiritual sight?
How do inner interpretations change the significance of a miracle account without necessarily settling every question about its outward occurrence?
What forms of transformation or steadfastness might deserve the attention we often give to extraordinary events?

neighbors.invitation: Read new birth through a change in qualities and character.
Consider prophetic signs turned into a summons to arise and serve.

references.label: 1 · John 9:1–7 · A man born blind
references.note: John narrates a healing through clay and washing after Jesus rejects the disciples’ proposed blame of the man or his parents. Compare the narrative with the compilation’s spiritual interpretations of sight. Keep the narrated event, its interpretation, and its possible use as evidence distinct.

subjects.displayTitle: The golden rule: widening the circle of concern
subjects.introduction: Wish for your brother what you wish for yourself: the old rule looks simple until ‘Abdu’l-Bahá traces how a soul’s concern grows, from itself to its family, its city, its nation, and at last to the whole of humankind, which alone He calls perfection. Bahá’u’lláh applies the measure everywhere. To what we ascribe to others and what we would bear to hear said of us; to promises; to kings who rob their peoples to rear palaces; to the humble workman whose injustice weighs as heavily as a tyrant’s. Then He presses past reciprocity altogether, asking that we prefer our neighbor’s welfare to our own and seek it without thought of reward. Confucius, asked for one word to guide a life, answered with reciprocity and the refusal to impose on others what one would not want oneself [1]; the comparison shows both the kinship of the traditions and the further step the Bahá’í teaching takes. The circle widens next toward consorting with all in kindness and love, toward loving one’s enemies, and toward service to others.
subjects.arc: Begin with the widening of concern, apply reciprocity to speech and public responsibility, then move through generosity toward service without reward.

order.why: Read regard for another as a requirement of human kinship.
shortened: The children of men are all brothers, and the prerequisites of brotherhood are manifold. Among them is that one should wish for one's brother that which one wisheth for oneself.

order.why: Open with concern expanding from self to all humanity.
shortened: Every imperfect soul is self-centred and thinketh only of his own good. But as his thoughts expand a little he will begin to think of the welfare and comfort of his family. If his ideas still more widen, his concern will be the felicity of his fellow citizens; and if still they widen, he will be thinking of the glory of his land and of his race. But when ideas and views reach the utmost degree of expansion and attain the stage of perfection, then will he be interested in the exaltation of humankind. He will then be the well-wisher of all men and the seeker of the weal and prosperity of all lands. This is indicative of perfection.

order.why: Ground mutual comfort in the image of one tree.
shortened: O people of the Bayan! Fear ye all together the Day when God desireth to take what is with you and give you what He pleaseth. This is the Day of Truth. Even as ye took before, so shall ye take, and even as ye return deposits one to another, so unto Him Whom God shall make manifest shall ye return what is with you.

order.why: Give that regard a concise expression.
Retain the direct command to be toward others as toward oneself.
Connect the refusal to wish harm with freedom from pride.
shortened: Wish not for others what ye wish not for yourselves; fear God, and be not of the prideful.

order.why: Apply reciprocity to what we ascribe and say.
Consider the words we would be willing to hear ourselves.
shortened: He must not wish for anyone that which he doth not wish for himself, nor speak that which he would not bear to hear spoken by another, nor yet desire for any soul that which he would not have desired for himself.

order.why: Join wishes for others with keeping promises.
shortened: He should not wish for others that which he doth not wish for himself, nor promise that which he doth not fulfill.

order.why: Distinguish the perspectives of justice and mercy.
shortened: The third word we have recorded on the third leaf of Paradise is this: "O son of man! If thine eyes be turned towards mercy, forsake the things that profit  thee, and cleave unto that which will profit mankind. And if thine eyes be turned towards justice, choose thou for thy neighbor that which thou choosest for thyself.

order.why: Apply the rule to rulers and the burdens placed on peoples.
Consider uprightness without self-preference.
shortened: It is Our wish and desire that every one of you may become a source of all goodness unto men, and an example of uprightness to mankind. Beware lest ye prefer yourselves above your neighbors.

order.why: Introduce the preference of another before oneself.
Explains willing preference of one’s neighbor to oneself, rather than compulsory equalization.
Examine welfare sought without an ulterior motive.
shortened: The difference between me and the rest is that I wish the welfare of the people for their own sakes and without any ulterior motive.

order.why: Read happiness linked to the well-being of others.
Consider the protection of others.
Move beyond personal opinions and personalities.
Read public spirit as an expression of service.
shortened: Man must be self-sacrificing in the service of the Cause of God and the diffusion of the Fragrances of God. Man must not be self-centered and self-occupied but public-spirited.

order.why: Retain the reported account of preference as a sign of sincerity.
Consider the challenge to self-occupation.
Read thoughtfulness as a quality of a believer.
Turn energy toward a neighbour’s education.
shortened: Forget your own selves, and turn your eyes towards your neighbor. Bend your energies to whatever may foster the education of men.

order.why: Consider the concrete work of illuminating and helping another.
shortened: Ye are ever thinking and mentioning how ye may kindle a light, bring a tree to fruition, illumine a heart, make an eye seeing, and make an ear hearing. This is the station of the noble ones, and this is the station of the righteous ones.

order.why: Close the linked readings with love directed toward the good of all.
Retain the supplied fragment of reciprocal desire.
Apply the principle to burdens placed on another soul.
Read justice across stations and occupations.
shortened: Justice is not limited, it is a universal quality. Its operation must be carried out in all classes, from the highest to the lowest. Justice must be sacred, and the rights of all the people must be considered. Desire for others only that which you desire for yourselves.

Each man has been placed in a post of honor, which he must not desert. A humble workman who commits an injustice is as much to blame as a renowned tyrant. Thus we all have our choice between justice and injustice.

order.why: Face the critique of a life absorbed in its own interests.
shortened: The people of the world are thinking of, by, and for themselves. They are promoting their own selfish interests and serving their own small causes. Each soul is attached to his own hobby and beating his own drum and soaring in the atmosphere of his own desire. If they speak they have some known or unknown objective point in view, if they eat and sleep they desire to be strengthened in order to advance their own ideas. In brief all their movements are dictated by obedience to self. They live, move and feel like unto the animals, self-centred, self-occupied, seeing nothing, believing in nothing beyond their five senses.

order.why: Read freedom from selfish bonds as a benefit to humanity.
Consider the reported comparison of reciprocity and preference.
shortened: It must be so that each friend should prefer others to himself; the others should be first to him.
His Holiness Christ said: 'Do unto others..', but his Holiness Baha'u'llah says--Prefer him to thyself.

order.why: Read preference, truthfulness, and justice together.
shortened: In all the Books, both past and future, He hath commanded that the believers and those who have turned towards Him should prefer others over themselves. They should make their paramount concern the vindication of truth and the elimination of falsehood, and should choose for their brethren what they choose for themselves.

order.why: Consider love of neighbour alongside love of God.
Retain the Gospel’s positive formulation.
Read the supplied Levitical saying and related references.
Keep the supplied rabbinic formulation with its citation.
Read the supplied Islamic formulation.
Include the supplied Mahabharata formulation.
Include the supplied Buddhist formulation.
Include the supplied Zoroastrian formulation.
Consider the role assigned to this shared ethic in peace.
End with devotion and action free from calculation of reward.

questions: How does the circle of concern described here challenge the boundaries of our ordinary sympathies?
What changes when reciprocity is applied to speech, promises, work, or the exercise of public power?
What similarities and differences emerge among refraining from harm, doing good, and preferring another’s welfare?
How might the Analects’ counsel become a lifelong practice rather than a phrase we already assume we understand?
How can we learn what another person needs without simply projecting our own preferences, and how might we act without expecting a return?

neighbors.invitation: Consider an account in which former enemies become brothers.
Explore renewal that expresses itself in cultivating the capacities of others.

references.label: 1 · Confucius, Analects, Book XV · Reciprocity as lifelong practice
references.note: Asked for a word that could guide an entire life, Confucius offers reciprocity and counsels against imposing on others what one would not want oneself. Compare this restraint with the collection’s positive calls to benefit others and its invitation to prefer their welfare.
